defs: Security model that assumes no implicit trust and continuously verifies identities, devices, context, and access requests.

course.learn: Zero Trust assumes that network location alone should not create trust. Every access request is evaluated using identity, device, context, policy, and least privilege, with continuous verification where possible.
course.why: Modern users and resources are distributed across cloud, remote, and internal environments, so a hard perimeter is no longer enough.
course.example: An employee on the corporate LAN still must authenticate, use a compliant device, and receive only the access needed for a specific application.
course.exam: Common clues: never trust/always verify, least privilege, microsegmentation, policy engine, policy enforcement point, adaptive access.

breakdown.explanation: Create small protected trust boundaries around specific resources instead of relying only on one large network perimeter.

course.learn: In Zero Trust, the control plane makes access decisions. It evaluates identity, policy, context, and threat information to decide whether a request should be allowed.
course.why: Separating decision logic from traffic enforcement makes access consistent and centrally governed.
course.example: A policy engine determines that a user on an unmanaged device may read email but may not access sensitive finance systems.
course.exam: Policy engine and policy administrator belong to the control plane; the PEP enforces the decision in the data plane.

breakdown.explanation: Evaluate identity and context dynamically rather than making a one-time static trust decision.

course.learn: The Zero Trust data plane is where approved communication actually occurs and where policy decisions are enforced. Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs) allow, deny, or limit traffic.
course.why: A good decision is useless unless the system can enforce it at the connection or resource boundary.
course.example: A gateway receives an allow decision from the policy system and permits the user to reach one application while blocking others.
course.exam: PEP is a data-plane clue. Policy decision logic is control plane.
